analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $17 an hour and ends subminimum wages for tipped and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The Raise the Wage Act of 2025 would raise the $7.25 federal minimum wage to $17 an hour, but since its April 2025 introduction it has drawn 176 cosponsors — all Democrats — and no action beyond a committee referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $17 an hour in yearly steps over six years, and after that automatically raise it along with the growth in the typical worker's pay. It would also phase out the lower minimum wage for tipped workers, the lower starting wage for teenagers, and the practice of paying workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage. The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, who would see their pay rise in scheduled steps to $17 an hour over six years and continue rising with median wages after that [S2]. Tipped workers would gain a gradually rising base wage until it reaches the full minimum, and they would get a clear legal right to keep their tips [S2]. Workers with disabilities who are currently paid under special subminimum-wage certificates would move onto rising wage floors and then onto the full minimum wage, with the program sunsetting entirely [S2]. Newly hired teenagers would keep a lower starting wage but only until their rate catches up to the full minimum, after which that exception disappears [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $17 an hour in six annual steps, then indexes it to the annual percentage increase in the median hourly wage so it no longer loses value by sitting unchanged for years.

Phases out the separate tipped minimum wage: the base wage for tipped employees rises from its current level to $17 over six years, after which tipped workers must simply be paid the regular minimum wage, and the bill writes into law that employees have the right to retain their tips.

Ends the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities: wage floors under Section 14(c) special certificates step up to the full minimum wage within five years, new certificates are banned, the program sunsets, and the Department of Labor must provide transition assistance to employers and workers.
Raises the teen training wage floor to $6.00 immediately and schedules the exception for newly hired workers under 20 for repeal once it catches up to the full minimum wage.
The bill has attracted 176 cosponsors, giving it the kind of House support that, if scheduled, could pass it; all 176 are Democrats.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers bear the direct cost: restaurants and food service would have to pay tipped staff a rising base wage until it reaches the full minimum, and retail, care work, agriculture, and other low-wage employers would see scheduled wage increases up to $17 an hour, with some of that cost passed on in prices or absorbed in lower hiring [S2]. Employers currently holding subminimum-wage certificates for workers with disabilities would lose that wage exemption and the program itself would end [S2]. Taxpayers and agencies face modest administrative costs for Department of Labor wage determinations and public notices [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill directly mandates large, scheduled increases in employers' labor costs — the minimum wage rises more than 130% from $7.25 to $17 over six years — which small businesses in low-wage sectors would have to absorb through prices, staffing decisions, or margins.

Ending the Section 14(c) subminimum-wage program is contested even among disability advocates: some argue that people with the most significant disabilities could lose paid work in sheltered employment. The bill itself acknowledges this by directing the Labor Department to provide transition assistance and referrals aimed at 'ensuring continuing employment opportunities' for affected workers.

Raising the tipped base wage toward the full minimum hits the restaurant industry hardest, since tipped workers currently can be paid a much lower base wage by their employers; industry groups typically argue this raises menu prices and squeezes independent restaurants.

Indexing to median wage growth is a one-way ratchet: the minimum wage can rise with the economy but there is no downturn mechanism, which critics say could compound cost pressures in weak labor markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and concentrated on the people with the least bargaining power: roughly 13 years after the last federal increase, workers at $7.25 would reach $17 within six years, and three long-standing carve-outs (tipped, teen, and disability subminimum wages) would be scheduled for repeal. The honest costs are real — higher labor bills for small restaurants and other low-wage employers, some price pass-through, and a genuine dispute within the disability community about ending sheltered subminimum work — and the bill tries to blunt them with long phase-ins, a tip-retention guarantee, and transition assistance. On balance the design is gradual and targeted; the main reason workers would not benefit is not the bill's flaws but the fact that it has not moved an inch in the House.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee the same day, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Representative Bobby Scott, the top Democrat on the Education and Workforce Committee, introduced the Raise the Wage Act of 2025 on April 8, 2025 with 176 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which is the committee that would normally write and advance minimum wage legislation.
That referral is the only action the bill has received; there is no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion movement recorded in its action history.

Because Congress is still in session, the bill remains alive on paper but has sat in committee for the entire time since introduction, which is where minimum wage bills from the minority party typically stall.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, employers of minimum-wage workers keep the current $7.25 federal wage, and the lower base wages for tipped workers and subminimum wages for workers with disabilities remain in place. Low-wage workers are no better off than they were in April 2025.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers of low-wage workers; wage stays $7.25

for.name: Rep. Robert C. 'Bobby' Scott
for.role: Ranking Member, House Committee on Education and Workforce; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Raise the Wage Act of 2025 and organized 176 cosponsors behind it.

for.name: 176 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including House leadership figures such as Rep. Hakeem Jeffries' caucus members and former Speaker Nancy Pelosi
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all 176 of them Democrats, making the bill the House minority's marquee minimum wage proposal.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: The committee has taken no action on the bill — no markup or committee vote — since it was referred on April 8, 2025.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor agenda
against.what_they_did: No Republican has cosponsored the bill, and with the majority controlling what reaches the floor, the bill has not been scheduled for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 176 cosponsors is a Democrat and no Republican has signed on, so at this stage support is entirely one-sided by party, though the bill has never come to a vote that would test where every member stands.

industries.note: The bill schedules the end of the tipped minimum wage, forcing employers to pay tipped staff a rising base wage until it reaches the full $17 minimum, plus a legal guarantee that workers keep their tips. Restaurant labor is the single biggest cost line affected, so the industry's interest in blocking the bill runs directly against the wage gains its workers would get.

industries.industry: Retail, care work, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Any employer paying near the $7.25 federal floor faces scheduled increases to $17 over six years plus automatic indexation afterward. Workers in these industries are the bill's main beneficiaries, so the employers' interest runs against their own employees' paychecks.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and disability service providers holding 14(c) certificates
industries.note: The bill bans new special certificates, raises wage floors for existing certificate holders each year, and sunsets the program that lets them pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage. Some providers argue the exemption lets them offer jobs to people with the most significant disabilities; the bill counters with transition assistance and referrals to competitive integrated employment.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with the committee chaired by the majority party, has no Republican cosponsors, and has seen no committee activity since April 2025. On the normal path, it will remain in committee without a markup or floor vote for the rest of the 119th Congress unless House control or the committee's agenda changes; minimum wage bills in this position almost never reach a vote in a divided Congress.
